title: DFS on Seoul: Real Streets Explode ⚡
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) traverse real city-like intersections, diving deep before it ever backtracks. You’ll see how DFS chooses a path based on adjacency order—then reveal why it can look “smart” but miss the shortest route.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps ⚡ What happens when DFS explores real city intersections first? 

In this visualization of DFS, each street intersection is a node and each road segment is an edge. The algorithm doesn’t “plan ahead”—it goes as deep as possible using a stack (explicit or via recursion), marking visited nodes to avoid loops. When the current branch dead-ends, DFS backtracks to the last junction and continues.

Deep technical breakdown (in 30 seconds):
• Graph = intersections (nodes) + streets (edges)
• DFS picks the next neighbor by traversal order (e.g., left/right/up/down)
• Visited prevents infinite cycling on real grids
• Output path depends heavily on neighbor ordering—not guarantees of shortest routes

Takeaway: DFS is great for reachability and deep exploration, but for shortest path you typically want BFS (or weighted algorithms like Dijkstra/A*).

Debate question: If neighbor order changes, should DFS be considered “the same algorithm” for routing outcomes?
